passage:
The school hall in the flooded town was crowded with mats and mattresses. Abhinav had been awake since five, and his hands were cracked from packing blankets. Every time someone asked for something, he wanted to say yes.
A woman was crying at the door because her mother’s medicines were left behind. Abhinav wanted to run out and find them himself.
Afreen, the camp coordinator, caught his sleeve. “Stay at the register. The trained boat team has the list of homes.” She wrote the woman’s address on a card.
Abhinav went back to his table. His shoulders dropped. He was still tired, but he was useful, and it was enough.

qa.q: How long had Abhinav been awake?
qa.a: Abhinav had been awake since five in the morning.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he wanted to run out and find the medicines himself?
qa.a: He was overwhelmed and eager to help, and every request made him want to say yes. He was also tired and might have put himself at risk.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Abhinav to stay at the register?
qa.a: Afreen said the trained boat team had the list of homes, so the address could reach people who knew how to go safely. Working inside the organised effort kept help effective and safe.

qa.q: How might the woman at the door have felt when Afreen wrote down her address?
qa.a: She was probably worried and relieved at once, since someone had taken her problem seriously. The passage shows only that she was crying and that her address was noted.

grounding: Shows a young adult volunteer in a flood camp feeling tired, useful and overwhelmed, and staying within an organised effort.

passage:
Dear Jomon,
It’s midnight and my hands are blistered. They gave me a green vest at the flood relief centre this morning and a job: counting and packing kits of rice, water and biscuits. I wanted to go where the water was. The coordinator said untrained people would only add to the rescuers’ worries, and pointed at the table.
So I packed for twelve hours. Around six a woman took a bag with both hands, without a word, and I nearly cried. In the van I couldn’t stop shaking, not from cold.
It doesn’t feel like much, but the lorries left full. I’ll write from home.
Siddharth

qa.q: How many hours did Siddharth pack kits?
qa.a: Siddharth packed kits for twelve hours.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth nearly cry when the woman took a bag?
qa.a: The woman took the bag with both hands and without a word, and it showed that the small job mattered. It touched Siddharth, who was tired and overwhelmed.

qa.q: Why did the coordinator's instruction to stay at the table make sense?
qa.a: Untrained people going into the water could add risk for the rescuers. Packing kits at the centre kept Siddharth's help useful and safe.

qa.q: How might the coordinator have felt telling Siddharth to stay at the packing table?
qa.a: The coordinator may have felt pressed and careful, wanting to use every helper well while keeping people safe. The passage shows only the instruction and the pointing to the table.

grounding: Shows a young adult volunteering in flood relief, tired and overwhelmed but useful within an organised effort.

passage: Jahnavi, you asked what the flood camp was really like. I'm Neelam, and I'm still tired, three weeks later. I went with the district relief team to a school turned into a shelter near Silchar. Four hundred people, one kitchen. I peeled potatoes till my fingers went white, sorted donated clothes, held babies so their mothers could sleep. One night I wanted to take a boat to a village I'd heard was cut off. The team lead said no: 'We don't send untrained people into currents. The rescue unit goes.' I was furious. The next morning the rescue unit brought eleven people back safely. I cried in the kitchen, from tiredness and relief. I felt useful and completely overwhelmed, both at once.

qa.q: How many people were in the shelter?
qa.a: Four hundred.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when the team lead refused the boat trip?
qa.a: Furious and frustrated, wanting to help the cut-off village directly.

qa.q: Why was the team lead's 'no' the right call?
qa.a: Untrained people in strong currents could become victims themselves; the trained rescue unit brought eleven people back safely.

qa.q: What might the mothers have felt when Neelam held their babies?
qa.a: Relieved and grateful to finally sleep in a crowded shelter.

grounding: A young volunteer in flood relief feels tired, useful and overwhelmed, and learns that working within the organised effort keeps help safe.

passage: Day one: when fever cases spread through the colony, Naveen signed up with the ward health team. His job was to go door to door with Pradeep, the health worker, checking for standing water and handing out leaflets. By evening he had visited sixty homes and felt useful and proud. Day three: an old man in Block D begged Naveen to take his feverish wife to hospital on his scooter. Naveen almost did, then remembered the team's rule: call the helpline and the team doctor. The ambulance came in twenty minutes. Naveen went home and sat in the dark, shaking, overwhelmed by how much was wrong. Day six: the team met. Pradeep showed a map: breeding spots down by half. 'Your street did that,' he told Naveen. Naveen slept properly for the first time that week.

qa.q: How many homes had Naveen visited by the end of day one?
qa.a: Sixty homes.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel sitting in the dark on day three?
qa.a: Shaken and overwhelmed by how much was wrong, after the scare with the feverish woman.

qa.q: What choice on day three kept the help safe and effective?
qa.a: Calling the helpline and the team doctor instead of taking the woman on his scooter, so the ambulance came in twenty minutes.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Naveen's work by day six?
qa.a: As genuinely valuable, pointing to the map and crediting Naveen's street for cutting the breeding spots.

grounding: Over a week a young volunteer in a health drive feels useful, then overwhelmed, and relies on the organised team's rules.

passage: Kalyani, you're leaving for the relief camp tomorrow? Let your Karthik mama tell you something from the big cyclone, when I was your age. I went to Nagapattinam with a college group, full of fire. On the first day I tried to do everything: carry sacks, cook, pull things out of damaged houses. By night I'd cut my hand on a tin sheet and was useless. The camp leader, a retired army nurse we called Mary aunty, sat me down. 'One job, done well, inside the team. That's how we save people.' She put me on the water-distribution line. Twelve days, same job, clean water for two thousand people. I was tired, and sometimes overwhelmed. But I was useful, and I was safe. Choose one job, and do it with the team.

qa.q: What job did Mary aunty give young Karthik?
qa.a: The water-distribution line.

qa.q: How did young Karthik feel at the end of the first day?
qa.a: Exhausted and frustrated, having hurt his hand trying to do everything.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made young Karthik's help effective and safe?
qa.a: Accepting one job inside the team, on the water line, instead of trying to do everything alone.

qa.q: What might Mary aunty have seen in young Karthik that first night?
qa.a: An eager but overstretched volunteer who would burn out or get hurt without a clear role.

grounding: An uncle recalls cyclone relief work, tiring and overwhelming, made useful and safe by one role inside an organised team.

passage: On the third day of the Silchar floods, the relief camp in the school building had no power after dark. Neelam had been handing out dry rations since six in the morning, her feet soaked through her sandals. Irfan, the volunteer coordinator, had one rule: nobody goes into the water on their own. At dusk a man ran in shouting that his neighbour's family was stuck on a roof two lanes away. Neelam's whole body wanted to run. She grabbed her torch. Irfan caught her arm. "Neelam. Write it down. Lane, house, how many people. The boat team goes, not you." She wrote it with shaking hands, and he radioed it through. Twenty minutes later the boat's lamp swung across the dark water. Neelam went back to the ration line, handed a packet to a crying girl, and suddenly had to sit down on the steps. Irfan brought her tea and said nothing.

qa.q: What was Irfan's one rule?
qa.a: Nobody goes into the water on their own.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she suddenly sat down on the steps?
qa.a: She was exhausted and overwhelmed after the long day and the fear for the family on the roof.

qa.q: Why was writing down the details wiser than running to the roof?
qa.a: It got the trained boat team there quickly while keeping Neelam safe, so the help stayed effective instead of adding another person to rescue.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt when he caught Neelam's arm?
qa.a: He was probably worried for her safety and firm about it, knowing the organised boat team could do more than one brave volunteer alone.

grounding: Shows a young flood-relief volunteer, tired, useful and overwhelmed, whose help stays safe and effective inside an organised effort.
